before: This paper replicates and extends selected findings from Duflo et al. (2012), who examine the effects of camera monitoring and attendance-linked pay on teacher attendance and student outcomes in nonformal education centers in rural India. Using the original replication data, I reproduce the estimated effects on school opening and three measures of children's recorded departure from their original centers. I then examine whether treatment effects on recorded departure differ according to children's baseline written-versus-oral test status. The extension finds that the treatment increased recorded departure by 26.1 percentage points among children who took the written baseline test, compared with 5.0 percentage points among those who took the oral test. The difference of 21.1 percentage points is statistically significant and remains so after adjustment for multiple testing. However, this heterogeneity is concentrated in residual departure rather than the recorded government-school marker. These results suggest that the effect of the intervention on recorded departure differed substantially across baseline groups, but they do not establish whether this difference reflects educational transitions, other forms of departure, or differences in measurement. In particular, the original departure measure depends on observations when schools were open, an outcome itself affected by treatment. The findings therefore provide evidence of heterogeneous effects on recorded operational departure, while highlighting the limitations of drawing broader conclusions about children's subsequent educational participation.
after: This paper replicates and extends selected findings from Duflo et al. (2012). I ask whether the effect of camera monitoring and attendance-linked pay on recorded departure differs according to children’s baseline written-versus-oral test status. Using the original replication data, I reproduce the effects on school opening and three recorded-departure outcomes. I then estimate treatment effects for baseline writers and nonwriters. The effect on recorded departure is 26.1 percentage points for writers and 5.0 points for nonwriters. The 21.1-point difference remains statistically significant after adjustment across the three departure outcomes. The residual-departure interaction is positive, while the government-school-marker interaction is imprecise. However, recorded departure depends on checks when schools were open, which treatment itself affected. These exploratory results show different effects on recorded departure across baseline groups; they do not establish whether children left education or transferred.
